result: The authors claim that imp-β-YFP forms a bright nuclear rim without RanGTP, which is substantially reduced but not eliminated by RanGTP, indicating that Ran modulates NPC interactions with both cargo-bound and free imp-β, and that at least a subset of NPC-bound transport receptors must be RanGTP-sensitive.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly requests 'raw data for the Imp-YFP experiment that is a part of Figure 1,' indicating concern about the presentation and interpretation of this data. The lack of raw data raises uncertainty about the strength of these claims, though the reviewers do not directly refute the conclusions.

result: The authors use FRAP experiments to demonstrate that imp-β has two pools at the NPC: one with rapid RanGTP-dependent turnover (16-fold faster recovery with RanGTP) and another that is stably bound for many minutes regardless of RanGTP presence.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'it is good to see that two different methods (FRAP, and photoconversion based FLAP) support their conclusion. With Ran, there is an enriched fast equilibrating pool of Imp-beta.' This indicates acceptance of the FRAP-based findings about two imp-β pools.

result: Photo-conversion experiments show that imp-β-mEos2 signal decays slowly (half-life 3-4 min) without RanGTP, and even with RanGTP some imp-β molecules remain at the pore for several minutes, supporting the existence of a stable imp-β pool.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that 'two different methods (FRAP, and photoconversion based FLAP) support their conclusion,' explicitly endorsing the photo-conversion data as corroborating evidence for the two-pool model.

result: dSTORM super-resolution imaging reveals two spatially separated pools of imp-β along the transport axis (~90 nm apart), with RanGTP markedly decreasing total localizations and changing the probability density function to show depletion from the nucleoplasmic face. Nup153 knockdown produces similar asymmetric depletion from the nuclear side.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises substantial concerns about Figure 3 data presentation and normalization: 'I have also some trouble following all conclusion and interpretations on this figure, as well as with some of the raw data and how it is displayed... How was the data normalized and displayed?' The reviewer questions whether technical artifacts (multiple emitter activation, localization precision differences) could explain the observed differences and notes inconsistencies in brightness between panels. The reviewer requests that authors 'Display the raw data. It is very crucial that you explain how the data was generated and normalized.'

result: Photobleach counting experiments show wild-type NPCs contain ~70 imp-β molecules without RanGTP, with RanGTP causing a 27% decrease. Nup153 knockdown reduces imp-β by 34% without RanGTP and 33% with RanGTP, suggesting most RanGTP-displaced imp-β is bound to Nup153.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses serious methodological concerns about the photobleach counting approach: 'While I do believe that overall reproducibility may be sufficient to make comparative analysis, I discourage of giving specific numbers... Stepwise bleaching analysis suffers from many problems that make determination of absolute abundance levels very, very difficult.' The reviewer lists multiple technical issues (out-of-focus contributions, YFP dark states, maturation time, homo-FRET) and states 'the true number of Imp-beta at the pore might easily be several folds off.' The reviewer requests that 'This figure also suffers from suboptimal presentation. It should be revised and clarified for the readers.'

result: In Nup153 knockdown cells, large cargos translocate the NPC faster under passive conditions (becoming less RanGTP-dependent), but active transport efficiency is reduced, indicating Nup153 affects both passive permeability and active transport.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'Transport experiments show that modulation by Ran alters both passive and active transport' and describes the manuscript as 'an exciting an impressive piece of work.' No specific concerns are raised about these transport experiments.

result: Imp-β (1 μM) significantly decreases NPC permeability for GFP probes, while RanGTP greatly increases permeability. TRN1 shows no strong effect on permeability even at 2 μM, and imp-β no longer restricts the NPC in Nup153 knockdown cells, suggesting the imp-β•Nup153 interaction specifically creates a steric barrier.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 affirms 'The current manuscript provides proof that RanGTP influences the permeability of the NPC itself' and calls it 'new interesting insights into the transport mechanism.' No concerns are raised about the permeability assays.

result: In vitro, imp-β and Nup153FG form large, higher-order complexes (micron-sized structures, tens to hundreds of imp-β molecules) that are entirely inhibited and even dissolved by RanQ69L•GTP, with Ran action occurring specifically through imp-β's Ran-binding domain.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'I have trouble following the logic of the motivation and description of these experiments in relation to the in vivo experiments' and notes the result 'does not come very much as a surprise, since Imp-beta has several binding sites for FG repeats.' The reviewer requests 'Show the exact concentration of the reagents for the procedures used' and critically asks for a control experiment testing Ran's effect on TRN1•Nup153FG complexes to 'help rationalize the data on Nup153-Impbeta.'

result: TRN1 also forms large complexes with Nup153FG in vitro, but unlike imp-β, these TRN1•Nup153FG complexes are insensitive to RanQ69L•GTP, demonstrating functional and biophysical distinction between TRN1 and imp-β despite both being transport receptors.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly requests an experiment to 'test the effect of Ran on Nup153G-transportin complex. This is an important control and will help rationalize the data on Nup153-Impbeta.' The reviewer questions 'how such a generic mechanisms can be rationalized in line with i) their finding that in vivo the Imp-beta and transportin are doing different things (and how this in vitro experiment is then supporting their conclusions).' This indicates the reviewer finds the TRN1 data insufficient to support the claimed specificity.

result: The authors propose a model where imp-β and Nup153 interact at the NPC's nuclear face to form a Ran-regulated meshwork/barrier that modulates NPC permeability, with the material forming via specific coordination between imp-β and FG domains and being dynamically sensitive to RanGTP.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the authors propose that impβ and Nup153 interact at the nuclear side of the NPC where they form a Ran-regulated meshwork' and calls this 'new interesting insights' that 'should be accepted for publication in eLife.' Reviewer 1 raises a minor terminological concern about using 'reminiscent' when comparing to FG gels, noting 'their potential gels are conceptually very different,' but does not reject the overall model.

result: The authors conclude that imp-β is a functional component of the NPC (not just a soluble transport receptor) based on its ability to alter pore permeability in a Ran-dependent manner and its stable residence at the NPC for minutes.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 endorses this interpretation, stating the manuscript 'provides proof that RanGTP influences the permeability of the NPC itself' and presents 'new interesting insights.' No reviewer challenges the functional component interpretation.

result: Single-pore resolution experiments reveal significant NPC-to-NPC variation in imp-β distribution, which may reflect variation in the instantaneous functional state of the cellular NPC pool.
evaluation: Neither reviewer raises concerns about the heterogeneity observations. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the single-pore resolution data in the context of discussing the waterfall plots.
